## Prevalence of Dark Patterns {.smaller visibility="hidden"}

<!-- recovered from ppt-archive/12-Compliance.pptx slide 65 -->
![](images/dark-pattern-prevalence-table.png){width="58%"}

**200 of 292 sites (68%)** use at least one. The leaders are **identity
confirmation** (24%), **unclear request receipt** (21%), and the **privacy maze** (19%).

::: {.notes}
The catalog of dark patterns and how often each appears, grouped by the three
families. The top three are worth naming: identity confirmation (prove who you are
before we stop selling your data), unclear request receipt (did it work? nobody
knows), and the privacy maze (the opt-out is somewhere in here). CAPTCHA, the example
students argued about earlier, is rare at under 3%. Cold-call: the three leaders are
all about information rather than visual trickery; what does that say about where
regulation should focus?
:::

## Distribution of Dark Patterns Across Opt-Out Control Methods {visibility="hidden"}

<!-- recovered from ppt-archive/12-Compliance.pptx slide 66 -->
![](images/dark-patterns-by-control-method.png){width="88%"}

::: {.notes}
Fig. 9 and Table 7: number of dark patterns per site for each control method, N=292,
and the top five patterns in each. Browser opt-out sites mostly have zero or one;
form sites peak at one or two; "both" sites peak at two. Forms lead with identity
confirmation (37.8%) and unclear request receipt (34.6%); browser opt-outs with cookie
control misdirection (18.8%) and asymmetry (14.3%); "both" with the privacy maze
(43.4%) and identity confirmation (37.7%).
:::

## Distribution of Dark Patterns Across Third-Party Platforms {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="64%"}
<!-- recovered from ppt-archive/12-Compliance.pptx slide 67 -->
![](images/dark-patterns-by-third-party.png)
:::
::: {.column width="36%"}
- Of 292 sites, **37%** use OneTrust, **7.5%** another vendor, **55%** built their own
- Sites with **no vendor** cluster at zero or one dark pattern; **OneTrust** sites
  cluster at **two**
- Top OneTrust patterns: identity confirmation (35%), verified email (33%), privacy
  maze (29%), baked into the default flow
- Paying for compliance tooling is not compliance: the **vendor irony**
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Fig. 10 and Table 8: number of dark patterns per site by third-party platform, N=292,
and the top five patterns in each. This is the single most surprising figure in Study
2, so give it a beat. Same axes across the three panels. The in-house sites are mostly
at zero or one; the OneTrust sites have a hump at two and a longer tail. Nobody is
accusing OneTrust of malice; the point is that the vendor's default request flow asks
for identity confirmation and a verified email, and most customers never change the
defaults. That is why the enforcement-gap slide calls it an irony: the site paid for
compliance and got a worse opt-out than the site that wrote its own. Other third
parties lead with identity confirmation (50.0%). Cold-call: who should the regulator
fine, the site or the vendor, and what would each do differently?
:::

## Discussion {.smaller visibility="hidden"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="30%"}
**Effectiveness of the CCPA**

- Seems to improve since the CPRA went into effect
- However, many websites still fail to comply with the CCPA
:::
::: {.column width="36%"}
**Challenges of measuring CCPA non-compliance**

- Human-intensive and time-consuming to examine the opt-out process
- Challenges of defining a dark pattern
- Challenges of verifying whether an opt-out request is complied with and fully
  executed
:::
::: {.column width="34%"}
**Recommendations**

- Regulators should take action to enforce the law
- Policy makers need clearer guidelines and more specific requirements, and should
  draft the law to make it easy to compliance-check websites' opt-out processes
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Three threads. Effectiveness: compliance seems to improve since the CPRA, but many
websites still fail. Measurement challenges: examining opt-out processes is
human-intensive and slow, defining a dark pattern is hard, and verifying that a
request was complied with and fully executed is harder still. Recommendations:
regulators should enforce the law, and policy makers should write clearer, more
specific requirements that make opt-out processes easy to compliance-check. The 2026
Disney and GM settlements are the first recommendation starting to happen.
:::

# Why Automated Compliance Is Hard {.center}

## The Enforcement Gap {.smaller}

- **Determining coverage** is hard: key thresholds rely on **non-public** data
- **Presence ≠ function:** a compliant-looking link may not work
- **Third-party irony:** sites pay vendors (e.g., **OneTrust**) and are *still* out
  of compliance; misconfiguration? no testing? willful neglect? hard to tell
- **The statute is silent** on many real patterns (CAPTCHAs, ambiguous receipts)
- **Willful evasion vs. honest oversight** is often **indistinguishable from the outside**

This is why **regulators**, not just scrapers, are needed, and why 2026's
enforcement turn toward *functional* opt-out matters.

::: {.notes}
Tie the whole class together. Determining coverage is hard because key thresholds
use non-public data. Presence does not equal function. Third-party irony: sites pay
vendors like OneTrust and are still out of compliance because of misconfiguration or
no functional testing. The statute is silent on many real patterns, and willful
evasion is often indistinguishable from honest oversight from outside. That last point
is the division of labor: automated measurement finds the haystack, but the final
call, covered? willful? legitimate security?, needs human and legal judgment. Natural
breakout prompt: if you were the CPPA, would you fund a permanent continuous auditing
program, or hire more lawyers? The 2026 enforcement turn toward functional opt-out is
why the answer is starting to look like "both". Route to the compliance breakout.
:::

## What Measurement Tells Policy {.smaller}

- Compliance is **rising but incomplete**; ~45% fail even appearance rules
- **Spillover is real** (78% extend opt-out nationwide): a strong state law can set
  a national floor
- **~30%** of opt-out attempts fail outright; most sites use **at least one dark pattern**
- Banning dark patterns **on paper** (CPRA) is not the same as **eliminating** them

**Open questions:** automatically verify an opt-out actually *worked*? Detect dark
patterns at scale? Distinguish evasion from error?

::: {.notes}
Land on the meta-point: empirical measurement is how we hold privacy law accountable
to its own promises. The 2026 GM ($12.75M) and Disney ($2.75M) settlements are
enforcement catching up to what these two studies documented in 2023 and 2024:
measurement finds the pattern, enforcement litigates one instance of it. The open
research questions are the natural bridge forward: can we automatically verify that an
opt-out actually worked? detect dark patterns at scale? distinguish willful evasion
from honest error? Bridge back to the federal-vs-state debate and forward to the AI
and privacy meeting.
:::

## Summary of Findings {.smaller visibility="hidden"}

- **RQ1: Can consumers successfully exercise their opt-out rights?**
  Nearly 30% of the attempted opt-out requests could not be submitted, did not
  succeed, or had unclear status updates.
- **RQ2: What does it take for a consumer to submit an opt-out request? Do
  opt-out processes violate CCPA requirements?**
  The opt-out process varies widely depending on website categories, opt-out
  control methods, and third-party platforms handling the opt-out process on
  behalf of the websites. Some sites allow submission with just a few clicks,
  while others require a lengthy process and significant personal information.
- **RQ3: What types of dark patterns are used in the opt-out process? Are they
  violating CCPA requirements, or exploiting loopholes the CCPA has not addressed?**
  Multiple types of dark patterns are found in the opt-out process. Although some
  are clearly prohibited by the CCPA, others are not explicitly addressed by it.
- **RQ4: What are the characteristics of the websites that employ dark patterns?**
  Most websites implement at least one type of dark pattern. Sites with different
  opt-out control methods and third-party platforms tend to exhibit different
  types of dark patterns.

::: {.notes}
Close on the four findings. The original deck has a draft "Conclusions" slide listing
the first three questions without answers immediately before this one; it is folded
into this slide.
:::

# Discussion {.center}

Pick a website you used **today**. Find its opt-out. How many clicks? What does it ask
for? Which **dark pattern family**, if any, and is it a **violation** or a **loophole**?

::: {.notes}
Cold-call prompt as written on the slide: pick a site, walk the class through the
click count and any dark patterns encountered. Best-in-class exercise: enable GPC in
Safari or Firefox (Do Not Sell or Share toggle, about ten seconds), then load a site
you use daily and watch, via Privacy Badger or the dev-tools Network tab, whether
third-party behavior actually changes. Route students to the Web Tracking hands-on
activity to do this systematically, and to the compliance breakout for the extended
dark-patterns edge-case discussion. Debate seed: should state AGs and the CPPA fund
continuous automated auditing on the model of Study 1, or is enforcement better served
by targeted litigation on the model of the Disney and GM cases? Land the meta-point:
the enforcement gap closes when measurement and litigation move together.
:::
